name: Orthodontic retainer

lead: A retainer holds teeth in place after braces or aligners, either as a removable plastic or wire device or a wire bonded behind the teeth.
Its evidence is for keeping teeth aligned. Forum claims that retainers help or block jaw and palate growth have not been studied.

paras: Passive pressure or a bonded wire keeps teeth from drifting back while surrounding fibres adapt.
Poor hygiene can cause decay or gum inflammation; bonded retainers can cause unwanted tooth movement (wire syndrome); removable ones can break or warp.

lead: An orthodontic retainer is a custom appliance, either removable (wire-and-acrylic Hawley or clear vacuum-formed plastic) or fixed (a wire bonded behind the front teeth), worn after braces or aligners to hold teeth in their new positions [1][2]. Its purpose is to limit relapse, the tendency of teeth to drift back, which is attributed to periodontal fibre recoil, soft-tissue pressure, occlusion and continued growth [2].

Reviews of the orthodontic literature emphasise that retention should be planned in advance, may vary in duration, and depends on patient compliance [1]. In looksmaxxing forums, retainers are discussed mainly in relation to whether wearing or stopping them affects jaw, palate or facial growth, a claim for which the sources reviewed contain no supporting studies.
infobox: Set by the orthodontist; fixed or indefinite [2]

paras: Removable options include the Hawley retainer (metal wire with acrylic base, the oldest type), the clear vacuum-formed retainer, and variants of these [1][2]. Fixed retainers are wires bonded to the tongue side of the front teeth, requiring less patient cooperation but harder to clean [2]. Newer removable cases linked to a phone app track and remind wear [2].

Wikipedia notes that relapse is more likely when removable retainers are not worn consistently, that one cited review found Hawley retainers ineffective at preventing incisor crowding relapse, that vacuum-formed retainers appear better for lower incisors, and that fixed retainers gave the best retention [2]. A randomised trial examined whether audiovisual instructions and weekly reminders improved retainer wear compliance [3]. Cost and satisfaction comparisons of Hawley and vacuum-formed retainers have also been published [4].

Poor cleaning can lead to decay and gum inflammation, particularly with fixed retainers [2]. A systematic review describes "wire syndrome", unintended tooth movement that can occur even with an intact bonded retainer wire, as an undesirable event distinct from relapse [5].

Forum threads on looksmax.org ask whether long-term retainer wear removes the chance of natural forward growth [6], whether a bonded retainer harms facial structure [7], and whether retainers can be used to expand the palate or combined with mewing [8][9]. The orthodontic sources reviewed describe retainers as maintaining tooth position, not as growth-modifying appliances [1][2].

Randomised trials compare retainer types for compliance, cost and clinical performance [3][4][10]. A systematic review of bonded retainers documents wire syndrome as a complication [5]. No studies found on retainers affecting facial growth or appearance beyond tooth alignment.
